lesson.title: Forgetting and spaced retrieval

lead.text: Return to the 100 words. You lost 40 in the first day, and the 60 that remain are the ones that stuck best, so they go more slowly. Say 10 more go over the following week and a few more over the month after. Draw a graph of how much you can recall against the time since you learned the words, and the result is a curve that falls steeply at first and then flattens.

Hermann Ebbinghaus found this shape in the 1880s. He learned lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself after different delays. In 2015 Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros repeated the experiment with one volunteer and got a curve of the same shape, so the pattern has held up for well over a century.

The curve describes memory in general, and it does not fit every memory equally well. Some memories are strong and fall along a flat curve. Others are fragile and drop quickly. To make use of the curve we need a number that says which kind of memory we have.

steps.headline: A number for how long a memory lasts

lead.text: The number is called stability, written S. It is the number of days until the chance of recalling the memory has fallen to 90%. A memory with a stability of 3 days is still 90% likely to come back after 3 days. A memory with a stability of 30 days takes ten times as long to reach that point.

With S in hand, one formula gives the predicted recall R after t days: R = 1 ÷ (1 + t ÷ 9S). Here 9S means 9 × S. At t = 0 the fraction is zero and R = 1 ÷ 1 = 100%. As t grows the fraction grows and R falls, steeply at first and then more slowly, which is the curve Ebbinghaus found. Put t = S and the fraction is 1/9, so R = 1 ÷ (1 + 1/9) = 0.9, which matches the definition of S.

Take S = 3 days and look at day 18. Then 9S = 27 and t ÷ 9S = 18 ÷ 27 = 2/3. That gives R = 1 ÷ (1 + 2/3) = 3/5, which is 60%. The figure draws the whole curve for a memory with a stability of 3 days.

afterFigure.text: Press play and watch recall fall. Stability sits under the fraction, so a larger S makes t ÷ 9S grow more slowly and the curve flatter. A memory with a large stability fades slowly, and one with a small stability fades fast.

lead.text: A memory has a stability of S = 10 days. Use the curve R = 1 ÷ (1 + t ÷ 9S).

steps.headline: What a review does to a memory

lead.text: So far the memory has been left alone. Now suppose you test yourself on the words on day 4 and recall them correctly. A successful recall does two things. It lifts recall back to nearly 100%, as if the clock had restarted, and it raises the memory's stability, so the curve that follows is flatter than the one before.

Each success multiplies the stability by some factor. If a review multiplies it by 2.5, a memory with S = 2 days becomes one with S = 5 days, and forgetting from then on is two and a half times as slow. This is why reviews can be spaced further and further apart. The second review can wait longer than the first, and the third longer still.

Reviewing at widening gaps is called spaced practice, also known as distributed practice. The opposite is massed practice, which crams all the study into one session. The figure compares a memory reviewed on day 3 with one that is left alone.

afterFigure.text: The reviewed memory is back near 100% on day 3 and then declines far more slowly than the other. By the end of the month the gap between them is large, even though the reviewed memory cost only one short test.

steps.headline: Find predicted recall 15 days after a review that leaves stability at 5 days.

lead.text: A memory starts with a stability of 2 days. A review on day 4 triples it, from 2 days to 6 days. Now measure from that review.

steps.headline: Choosing the day of the next review

lead.text: A review that comes too early wastes effort, because the memory is still strong. One that comes too late finds it already faded. A good schedule picks the day when predicted recall has just fallen to a target, and a common target is 90%. Discere schedules reviews this way with FSRS, a scheduling model built on a forgetting curve like the one above.
Stability was defined as the days until recall falls to 90%, so a card with stability S is due S days after its last review. The 90% target needs no further calculation.

Success then multiplies S and the next gap grows. Take a card with S = 2 days, and suppose each success multiplies stability by 2.5. It is due after 2 days. Its stability then becomes 5, so the next review is due 5 days later, on day 7. Stability becomes 12.5 and the gap after that is 12.5 days. The gaps are 2, 5 and 12.5 days, each longer than the last.

afterFigure.text: Each dot in the figure is a review. After each one recall returns to nearly 100%, and each curve that follows is flatter, so the dots sit further and further apart. That widening is the pattern to expect from any spaced schedule.

lead.text: Reviews are scheduled for the moment that predicted recall falls to the 90% target.

There is one more choice to make about a review, which is how to do it. You can reread your notes, which feels smooth and familiar. Or you can close them and try to recall what they said, which feels harder and more uncertain. The second method is called retrieval practice, and it is the kind of review the stability story assumed, since a review there means a successful act of recall.

Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke compared the two in 2006. Students studied a passage and then either reread it or practised recalling it. Five minutes later the rereaders did better, recalling 81% of the ideas in the passage against 75%. If the test had stopped there, rereading would have looked like the better method.

The students were tested again a week later and the order reversed. Those who had practised recalling kept far more than those who had reread. Effortful recall feels worse at the time and lasts longer, so the feeling that rereading is going well is a poor guide to what will last. This is why good flashcard systems make you try to answer before they show you the card.
A week after studying, students who had practised recall were compared with students who had reread. The counts are in the picture.

lesson.orientation: Read a forgetting curve and see how each successful retrieval flattens it, as Discere's scheduler assumes.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You learn 100 new words. A day later you still know 60 of them, so you have lost 40. Then you stop revising.

The question is what happens over the following weeks. A natural guess is that you keep losing words at the same pace, another 40 the next day and nothing left by the third. Most people's experience says otherwise, since whatever survives the first day tends to last much longer. Memory fades along a curve with a definite shape, and that shape can be written down.

This lesson follows the 100 words through time. It starts with the curve and a number that says how long a memory lasts, then shows what one review does to that number. After that it works out when the next review should come, and it finishes by comparing rereading with testing yourself.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a forgetting curve and work out when a card is due after each successful review.

recap.keyIdea: Forgetting is fast at first and slows. Each successful retrieval raises stability, so reviews can be spaced further apart, and practising recall beats rereading for lasting memory.

blocks.text: Back at the 100 words, you found that a memory with stability 10 days is predicted to fall to 50% by day 90, and that a review on day 4 lifted recall on day 17.5 from about 51% to 80%. A week after studying, recall practice led rereading by 14 points.

recap.nextHook: A memory fades unless it is used. Some learning happens with no effort to remember at all, as when a dog that hears a bell before every meal starts to drool at the bell alone, and the next lesson starts there.

questions.prompt: A memory has stability S = 4 days. Using R = 1/(1 + t/9S), what percentage recall is predicted 108 days after learning?
hints: Take one over one plus the quotient.
questions.onCorrect: Divide the days by 9S, then put the ratio in the curve. A longer wait with smaller stability leaves less recall.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share forgotten. The question asks for the share still recalled.
That is t ÷ 9S, not recall. Put it into the curve.

questions.prompt: Studying in short sessions spread over days, rather than one long session, is called what kind of practice?
hints: It is the opposite of massed practice, or cramming.
questions.onCorrect: Spreading study over days is distributed, or spaced, practice, the opposite of cramming.

misconceptions.feedback: Massed practice is one long session. The question asks about study spread across days.

questions.prompt: A memory has stability 6 days. A successful review multiplies stability by 3. How many days after that review is the card next due, when recall falls to 90%?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The new stability is 6 × 3 = 18 days, and a card is due when recall falls to 90%, which is S days after the review.

questions.onCorrect: Success multiplies stability, and the card is due S days later, so the gap widens.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the old stability. A successful review has raised it.
That adds 3 instead of multiplying by it.

questions.prompt: Over the next day, what is most likely to happen?
hints: Is the loss steady, or does it slow down once the weakest memories are gone?
What has already been forgotten cannot be forgotten twice.

acceptedIdeas: You lose fewer than the 40 you lost on the first day.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: You lose fewer than 40: forgetting is fast at first and slows as time passes.

choices.label: You lose most of the 60 that are left.
You lose fewer than the 40 you lost on the first day.

questions.onCorrect: Forgetting slows as the weakest memories go first. You predicted the shape of the curve.

misconceptions.feedback: That assumes a steady rate of loss. The loss is greatest at the start.
Losing most of the remainder would make the second day worse than the first. The loss tends to be gentler.

questions.prompt: A memory has stability 2 days. How many days until its predicted recall falls to 90%?
hints: Stability is the number of days until recall falls to 90%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Stability is the days until recall falls to 90%, so 2 days.

questions.onCorrect: Stability is, by definition, the days until predicted recall falls to 90%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is when this memory halves. The question asks about the 90% point.
That multiplies by nine. The definition of S already marks the 90% point.

questions.prompt: What percentage recall does the curve predict 90 days after learning?
hints: Substitute into 1/(1 + t/9S) and convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Divide the days by 9S and put it in the curve: here the ratio reaches one and recall has halved.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of days. Put t ÷ 9S into the curve to get a percentage.
That divides t by S. The curve divides by nine times S.

questions.prompt: After a successful review, what happens to the next gap?
hints: Stability goes up after a success.

acceptedIdeas: The memory fades more slowly, so the next review can wait longer.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A success raises stability, so the curve flattens and the next gap grows.

choices.label: The memory fades faster, so reviews must be closer together.
Nothing changes, because every review is the same.
The memory fades more slowly, so the next review can wait longer.

questions.onCorrect: Success raises stability. A flatter curve means the next review can wait longer.

misconceptions.feedback: A success strengthens the memory. It does not make it more fragile.
Each success changes the stability, so the gaps can grow.

questions.prompt: Why does a larger stability slow forgetting?
hints: Look at which number sits under the fraction.

acceptedIdeas: It makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows more slowly as days pass.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A larger S makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows slowly and recall stays high longer.

choices.label: It makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows more slowly as days pass.
It makes t smaller, so fewer days have passed.
It adds a fixed amount to recall.

questions.onCorrect: S sits under the fraction. A bigger S makes the ratio grow more slowly, so recall holds up.

misconceptions.feedback: The days passed are not changed by S. Only the ratio is.
Recall is never added to. It falls as the ratio grows.

questions.prompt: What percentage recall is predicted 13.5 days after that review?
hints: Take one over one plus your answer.
questions.onCorrect: The review raised stability, so 9S is bigger and t ÷ 9S is smaller: recall stays high.

misconceptions.feedback: That stops after t ÷ 9S. Put it in the curve to get recall.
That is the share forgotten. The question asks for the share recalled.

questions.prompt: A card has stability 12 days. If reviews are scheduled for when predicted recall falls to 90%, how many days after its last review is it due?
hints: The 90% target matches that definition exactly.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Stability is defined as the interval at which predicted recall reaches 90%, so the card is due in 12 days.

questions.onCorrect: Stability is the days to reach the 90% target, so the card is due after that many days.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the target recall, not a number of days.
That multiplies by nine. The definition of S already includes the 90% target.

questions.prompt: A week after studying, students who practised recall remembered 56% of idea units and students who reread remembered 42%. How many percentage points higher was recall practice?
hints: Percentage points are a plain difference of percentages.
Subtract the rereading score from the recall-practice score.
questions.onCorrect: Recall practice looked worse early but lasted longer. The gap is a plain difference of the two scores.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the two scores. The question asks how far apart they are.
Percentage points are a difference, not a sum.
